There is no clear boundary between ocean and sky; pressure and temperature increase steadily with depth. Steam worlds are thought to be water worlds that have migrated too close to their stars. They are lethal to approach and useful chiefly as subjects of study.

variants.description: {World} has no distinct ocean surface, and its envelope passes gradually from steam to supercritical fluid with depth.
A boiling ocean lies beneath a dense steam atmosphere on {world}, with violent convection and constant cloud.

types.name: Ice world
types.entry: {World} is an ice world, a body whose surface is composed mainly of water ice, often mixed with rock dust and other frozen volatiles.
types.description: An ice world is a planet or moon whose surface is composed mainly of water ice, often mixed with rock dust and other frozen volatiles. Ice worlds are common beyond the snow line of every star system in the Basin and include many of the moons of its giants. Their surfaces range from ancient and heavily cratered to smooth and recently resurfaced, depending on whether the interior is still warm. Ice worlds supply water, oxygen and reaction mass to nearby installations and are the principal resource of systems such as Halyard.

variants.description: {World's} ice is darkened by rock dust and organic compounds, so that its surface is grey or brown rather than white. Dark ice absorbs more sunlight and is warmer than clean ice.
{World's} surface is clean, highly reflective ice that returns most of the light falling on it. It appears brilliant white from orbit and remains extremely cold.
Large areas of {world's} ice have been broken into rafts and blocks and refrozen in disordered positions, a sign of warm material or liquid water rising from below.

types.name: Subglacial ocean world
types.entry: {World} is a subglacial ocean world, a body with a liquid water ocean beneath a shell of ice kilometers thick. The ocean is kept liquid by tidal heating from a parent body, by radioactive decay in the rocky core or by some outside source of heat, and it may be in contact with the rock below, where chemical reactions can support life.
types.description: A subglacial ocean world is a planet or moon with a liquid water ocean beneath a shell of ice kilometers thick. The ocean is kept liquid by tidal heating from a parent body, by radioactive decay in the rocky core or by some outside source of heat, and it may be in contact with the rock below, where chemical reactions can support life. Settlements are built on or within the ice, with shafts sunk to reach the ocean. Such worlds hold large reserves of water and, in some cases, lattice in the rock beneath. Halvard's Rest, the refinery moon of Mercer-Ibarra, and the rogue worlds of the Hollows, warmed by Absent heat engines, are subglacial ocean worlds.

variants.description: The ice covering {world's} ocean is only a few kilometers thick, and the ocean can be reached by drilling. Cracks and ridges on the surface mark places where water has risen close to it.
The ice covering {world's} ocean is tens of kilometers thick, and the ocean beneath it has been detected only by its effect on {world's} rotation and magnetic field.
Hydrothermal vents on the floor of {world's} ocean release heat and dissolved minerals, supporting communities of life in complete darkness.
{World's} ocean is kept liquid by heat from a source outside any natural system, in the absence of a star or a tidal partner.

types.name: Cryovolcanic world
types.entry: {World} is a cryovolcanic world, an icy body with active volcanism in which the erupting material is water, ammonia or methane rather than molten rock.
types.description: A cryovolcanic world is an icy planet or moon with active volcanism in which the erupting material is water, ammonia or methane rather than molten rock. Cryovolcanoes and geysers resurface the world, and the most energetic of them vent material to orbit, where it may feed a ring around the parent planet. Plumes carry samples of subsurface liquid to the surface, making cryovolcanic worlds the easiest places to study their hidden oceans.

variants.description: Fields of erupting jets cluster along zones of tidal stress on {world}, venting water vapor and ice grains high above the surface.
Large domes of extruded ice rise from {world's} plains, formed by slow eruptions of thick, cold slurry.
Flows of ammonia and water spread across {world's} surface from fissures, freezing into smooth, lobed plains.

types.name: Methane-sea world
types.entry: {World} is a methane-sea world, a cold body with a thick nitrogen atmosphere, an orange organic haze and lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane.
types.description: A methane-sea world is a cold planet or moon with a thick nitrogen atmosphere, an orange organic haze and lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane. It has a full hydrological cycle in which hydrocarbons take the place of water: rain falls, rivers run and erosion shapes the land, all at temperatures far below the freezing point of water. The bedrock is water ice. Methane-sea worlds are rich in organic chemistry and valued as sources of hydrocarbon feedstock and nitrogen.

variants.description: {World's} hydrocarbon seas are concentrated around its poles, while its equatorial regions are dry.
Organic haze in {world's} atmosphere is thick enough that the surface is seldom visible from orbit except at infrared wavelengths.
Long dunes of organic sand girdle {world's} equatorial regions, shaped by steady winds.

types.name: Hydrocarbon world
types.entry: {World} is a hydrocarbon world, a cold body on which heavier hydrocarbons predominate at the surface: seas of tar, dunes of waxy solids and plains of bitumen.
types.description: A hydrocarbon world is a cold planet or moon on which heavier hydrocarbons predominate at the surface: seas of tar, dunes of waxy solids and plains of bitumen. Its atmosphere is usually thin and its chemistry slower and more viscous than that of methane-sea worlds. Hydrocarbon worlds are potential sources of chemical feedstock, though extraction at their temperatures is difficult and energy-intensive.

variants.description: Viscous seas of tar fill {world's} lowlands, moving only slowly and freezing almost solid in winter.
Dunes of solid paraffin-like compounds cover large regions of {world}, soft and slippery underfoot.

types.name: Snowball world
types.entry: {World} is a snowball world, a planet that once had a temperate climate and has since frozen over entirely, following a change in its star's output, its orbit or its atmosphere.
types.description: A snowball world is a planet that once had a temperate climate and has since frozen over entirely, following a change in its star's output, its orbit or its atmosphere. Ice now covers its former oceans and continents, and its surface reflects so much light that recovery is difficult without outside intervention. Traces of former oceans, rivers and life may lie preserved beneath the ice, and such worlds are of considerable interest to survey.

variants.description: {World's} oceans have frozen to great depth, possibly to the seafloor, and the former coastlines lie under ice.
Remains of a former biosphere lie preserved beneath {world's} ice, from microorganisms to the structures of larger life.
A narrow band of open water and slush persists around {world's} equator, where some native life survives.

types.name: Hydrogen-ocean world
types.entry: {World} is a hydrogen-ocean world, a planet with a deep water ocean beneath a thick atmosphere of hydrogen. The hydrogen acts as a powerful greenhouse blanket and can keep the ocean liquid far beyond the distance at which an ordinary planet would freeze.
types.description: A hydrogen-ocean world is a planet with a deep water ocean beneath a thick atmosphere of hydrogen. The hydrogen acts as a powerful greenhouse blanket and can keep the ocean liquid far beyond the distance at which an ordinary planet would freeze. The atmosphere is not breathable, but the ocean beneath may host marine life of an unusual kind. Hydrogen-ocean worlds are candidates for biological survey and sources of hydrogen and water.

variants.description: {World's} ocean remains liquid far beyond its star's normal habitable zone, warmed by the insulating effect of its hydrogen atmosphere.
{World} has no star, or orbits so far from one that it receives almost no light, and its ocean is warmed by internal heat alone.

types.name: Hot giant
types.entry: {World} is a hot giant, a gas giant orbiting very close to its star, with an atmosphere heated to well over a thousand degrees.
types.description: A hot giant is a gas giant orbiting very close to its star, with an atmosphere heated to well over a thousand degrees. Hot giants are often inflated to radii larger than their mass would suggest, and many are losing atmosphere to the star. Their day sides are free of cloud and their night sides glow with their own heat. They usually orbit in a few days and are locked with one face toward the star. Their presence close to a star tends to clear the inner system of smaller planets.

variants.description: {World's} radius is substantially larger than its mass would suggest, its atmosphere swollen by heating from the star and from within.
{World} is losing atmosphere to its star, and the escaping gas forms a visible tail trailing behind it in its orbit.

types.name: Silicate-cloud giant
types.entry: {World} is a silicate-cloud giant, a very hot gas giant whose cloud deck is composed of silicate and iron condensates rather than water or ammonia.
types.description: A silicate-cloud giant is a very hot gas giant whose cloud deck is composed of silicate and iron condensates rather than water or ammonia. Such giants absorb most of the light that falls on them and appear dark by day, while their night sides glow a dull red. Their weather includes winds of extreme speed and precipitation of molten rock and iron at depth.

variants.description: Droplets of molten iron condense and fall through {world's} deep atmosphere, re-evaporating before they reach any surface.
{World} reflects almost none of the light that falls on its day side and appears nearly black against its star.

types.name: Cloudless giant
types.entry: {World} is a cloudless giant, a gas giant whose temperature lies between the condensation points of ammonia and of water, so that neither forms clouds in its upper atmosphere.
types.description: A cloudless giant is a gas giant whose temperature lies between the condensation points of ammonia and of water, so that neither forms clouds in its upper atmosphere. Without a cloud deck, the deep atmosphere scatters light much as a clear sky does, and the giant appears a deep, uniform blue. Cloudless giants are uncommon and visually distinctive, and their clear atmospheres make them useful references for long-range survey.

variants.description: {World} appears a deep, uniform blue from orbit, without visible banding or storms.
Traces of sodium and potassium in {world's} upper atmosphere form a thin haze that tints its blue toward violet.

types.name: Warm giant
types.entry: {World} is a warm giant, a gas giant at a moderate distance from its star, warm enough for its upper cloud deck to consist of water vapor.
types.description: A warm giant is a gas giant at a moderate distance from its star, warm enough for its upper cloud deck to consist of water vapor. Warm giants are highly reflective and appear bright white. They frequently lie within or close to their star's habitable zone, and their larger moons may therefore be warm enough to hold liquid water and life of their own.

variants.description: Bright decks of water-vapor cloud cover {world}, reflecting most of the light that falls on them and giving it a brilliant white appearance.
{World} orbits within its star's habitable zone, and its larger moons receive enough light and heat to hold liquid water at their surfaces.

types.name: Cold giant
types.entry: {World} is a cold giant, a gas giant in the outer part of its star system, with an upper atmosphere cold enough for clouds of ammonia and ammonium compounds.
types.description: A cold giant is a gas giant in the outer part of its star system, with an upper atmosphere cold enough for clouds of ammonia and ammonium compounds. It is the commonest class of giant in the Basin. Its cloud deck is divided into alternating light zones and dark belts by fast zonal winds, and large storms, some lasting for centuries, form along the boundaries between them. Cold giants typically have extensive systems of moons and rings. Halvard, which carries a stationary storm larger than Tallis, is a cold giant.

variants.description: {World's} clouds are organized into distinct light zones and dark belts in shades of tan, cream and brown, with turbulent eddies along their edges.
{World's} appearance is dominated by one or more storms larger than terrestrial planets, persisting for years or centuries.
{World's} bands are muted and its storms weak, giving it a pale, washed-out appearance.

types.name: Low-density giant
types.entry: {World} is a low-density giant, a gas giant with an unusually low mean density, its atmosphere extended far beyond what its mass would ordinarily hold.
types.description: A low-density giant is a gas giant with an unusually low mean density, its atmosphere extended far beyond what its mass would ordinarily hold. Some low-density giants are young and still contracting after formation; others are being inflated by heating or tidal forces. Most are losing atmosphere to space, and their extended envelopes make them susceptible to disruption.

variants.description: {World's} mean density is comparable to that of light foam, its envelope extending to a radius far beyond that of other giants of similar mass.
{World} is still contracting after formation and radiates more heat than it receives from its star.

types.name: Helium giant
types.entry: {World} is a helium giant, a gas giant whose atmosphere is dominated by helium rather than hydrogen. Such worlds are thought to form when a hot giant loses most of its hydrogen to stellar heating over a long period, leaving the heavier helium behind.
types.description: A helium giant is a gas giant whose atmosphere is dominated by helium rather than hydrogen. Such worlds are thought to form when a hot giant loses most of its hydrogen to stellar heating over a long period, leaving the heavier helium behind. Without the methane absorption that colors most giants, helium giants appear grey or white.

variants.description: {World's} cloud decks are a featureless grey-white, without the colors or banding typical of hydrogen giants.
{World} is the depleted remnant of a former hot giant, smaller and denser than it once was.

types.name: Ice giant
types.entry: {World} is an ice giant, a giant planet composed mostly of water, ammonia and methane above a rocky core, beneath a comparatively thin envelope of hydrogen and helium.
types.description: An ice giant is a giant planet composed mostly of water, ammonia and methane above a rocky core, beneath a comparatively thin envelope of hydrogen and helium. Methane in the upper atmosphere absorbs red light and gives ice giants their blue to blue-green color. Ice giants are common in the outer reaches of Basin systems; they have faint ring systems and families of small, icy moons, and their interiors may hold layers of superionic water.

variants.description: Methane absorption gives {world} a deep blue color, with occasional dark storms and bright high clouds.
{World} is a paler, hazier blue-green, its features softened by a high-altitude haze.
{World's} rotation axis lies close to the plane of its orbit, so that each pole spends decades in continuous daylight and then in darkness.

types.name: Mini-Neptune
types.entry: {World} is a mini-Neptune, a small gaseous planet, between about two and four times the radius of Earth, with a deep atmosphere of hydrogen and helium over a rocky or icy core and no accessible surface.
types.description: A mini-Neptune is a small gaseous planet, between about two and four times the radius of Earth, with a deep atmosphere of hydrogen and helium over a rocky or icy core and no accessible surface. Mini-Neptunes are among the commonest planets in the galaxy and in the Basin. Their atmospheres may conceal oceans of water or supercritical fluid at depth.

variants.description: A high-altitude photochemical haze shrouds {world}, obscuring the deeper atmosphere and giving it a featureless appearance.
A deep layer rich in water lies beneath {world's} hydrogen envelope, possibly as an ocean of supercritical fluid.

types.name: Dwarf planet
types.entry: {World} is a dwarf planet, a body massive enough to have been pulled into a rounded shape by its own gravity but too small to have cleared its orbit of other material.
types.description: A dwarf planet is a body massive enough to have been pulled into a rounded shape by its own gravity but too small to have cleared its orbit of other material. Dwarf planets are common in the outer belts of Basin systems and in the belts of some inner systems. The icy examples may hold thin, seasonal atmospheres of nitrogen or methane that freeze onto the surface when the body is far from its star.

variants.description: {World} is composed of ice and rock, its surface coated in nitrogen and methane frost that sublimates and refreezes with the seasons.
{World} is composed of rock and metal and lies in an inner asteroid belt, cratered and airless.

types.name: Comet
types.entry: {World} is a comet, a small body of ice, dust and rock. When its orbit carries it close to its star, the ices sublimate, forming a coma around the nucleus and tails of dust and gas that stream away from the star.
types.description: A comet is a small body of ice, dust and rock. When its orbit carries it close to its star, the ices sublimate, forming a coma around the nucleus and tails of dust and gas that stream away from the star. Comets captured into stable orbits around planets serve as convenient sources of water in systems without ice moons. Halyard's outer systems are crowded with comets, and they supply much of the trailing arm's water and reaction mass.

variants.description: {World} is venting jets of gas and dust from its surface, and it carries a coma and developing tail.
{World's} surface volatiles are exhausted, and a dark crust of residue seals the ice beneath it.
{World} has been captured into a stable orbit around a planet, where it no longer approaches its star closely enough to become active.

types.name: Moonlet
types.entry: {World} is a moonlet, a small, irregular moon or rock, usually a captured asteroid or a fragment of a larger body. Moonlets lack the gravity to pull themselves into a rounded shape, and their surface gravity is too weak to hold loose material securely.
types.description: A moonlet is a small, irregular moon or rock, usually a captured asteroid or a fragment of a larger body. Moonlets lack the gravity to pull themselves into a rounded shape, and their surface gravity is too weak to hold loose material securely. They are convenient anchors for stations, docks and moorings. The port at Sable is built from hulls moored around the largest of its dark moonlets.

variants.description: {World} is a captured asteroid in an irregular, often inclined orbit, its composition unrelated to the planet it orbits.
{World} orbits at the edge of a ring and its gravity keeps the ring's boundary sharp.
{World's} carbon-rich surface reflects almost no light, and it is difficult to see against the sky.

features.description: {World's} rotation is locked to the planet it orbits, so that one hemisphere permanently faces its parent and the other faces away. From the near side the parent hangs fixed in the sky, waxing and waning through its phases.

{World} follows a markedly elongated orbit, and the light and heat it receives vary considerably between its closest and farthest approaches to its star. Seasons are governed more by distance than by axial tilt and are unequal in length.
{World} orbits in the opposite direction to its parent's rotation and to most other bodies in its system. A retrograde orbit usually indicates that {world} was captured rather than formed in place.
{World's} orbital period stands in an exact whole-number ratio to that of one or more neighbors, so that their alignments repeat on a fixed schedule.
features.example: The Orrery's nine worlds are bound in a mutual resonance of this kind.

features.description: {World} forms a binary pair with a body of comparable size, the two orbiting a common center that lies in the space between them. Each is prominent in the other's sky, and both share an orbit around their star.
{World} shares its orbit with a much larger body, holding a stable position sixty degrees ahead of or behind it. Debris and smaller bodies often collect in the same region.
{World} did not form in its present orbit but was captured from elsewhere, and its composition differs from that of its neighbors.

{World's} axis is tilted so far that its poles in turn face directly toward the star. Each hemisphere passes through months of continuous daylight followed by months of darkness, and seasonal extremes are severe.
{World} rotates slowly, with a day lasting weeks or longer. Its surface heats strongly through the long day and cools deeply through the long night.
{World} rotates rapidly, with a day of only a few hours. It is visibly flattened at the poles, and its weather is organized into narrow, fast-moving bands.
{World} orbits close to its star, completing a revolution in a matter of days or weeks. The star dominates the sky, and the heat and radiation it delivers shape every aspect of the surface.
{World} orbits far from its star, which appears in its sky as a bright point rather than a disc. Sunlight at the surface is weak, and a single orbit takes many decades to complete.
{World} orbits a close pair of stars rather than a single star, circling both at once. The two suns rise and set together, and their mutual eclipses periodically dim the daylight.
{World's} year lasts many times longer than a standard year, so that each season persists for longer than a human generation spends in one place.
{World's} year lasts only a few weeks, and its seasons, if it has any, pass too quickly for agriculture to follow them.

{World} tumbles irregularly rather than spinning about a fixed axis, so that the length of its day and the position of its poles change unpredictably. Navigation and timekeeping on the surface are difficult.
{World} rotates a whole number of times for every few orbits of its star, so that the same hemispheres face the star at each closest approach. Its day is long and its solar day longer still.
{World's} orbit is steeply inclined to the plane in which the other bodies of its system move, and it passes high above and below them in the course of each revolution.
{World's} orbit is changing measurably over centuries under the influence of its neighbors, and survey records show it closer to or farther from its star than it was when first charted.
{World} has no moons, and its night sky is lit only by the stars and by other planets of its system.
A single large moon orbits {world}, prominent in its sky and strong enough to raise tides and stabilize its axis.
Dozens of moons orbit {world}, most of them small and captured, and several are visible in its sky at any time.
Small shepherd moons orbit {world} at the edges of its rings, keeping their boundaries sharp.
Two of {world's} moons share an orbit, exchanging places periodically as one overtakes the other.
Many of {world's} moons are captured bodies in distant, inclined and often retrograde orbits.
One of {world's} moons is habitable in its own right, warmed by the star and by tidal flexing.
{World's} parent planet fills a large part of its sky, passing through phases and casting eclipses across the surface.
A small moon orbits {world} itself, a rare arrangement that is stable only in particular conditions.
{World's} moons regularly pass in front of its star, so that eclipses are frequent and well known to anyone living on the surface.

A system of rings encircles {world}, composed of ice, rock or dust and divided into bands by gaps and the influence of small moons. The rings are visible across the sky from {world's} surface and from its moons.

{World} is exposed to intense radiation from its star, a stellar remnant or trapped radiation belts. Unshielded electronics degrade quickly, and surface work requires shielding and close monitoring of exposure.
{World} has a strong magnetic field that deflects much of the stellar wind and traps charged particles in belts around it. The belts are hazardous to cross but protect the surface.
Aurorae are frequent and bright in {world's} skies, sometimes reaching far from the poles. They are visible on most nights and can disturb communications.
{World} is steadily losing atmosphere to space, driven by heating or stellar wind. The escaping gas can be detected around {world} and, in extreme cases, seen as a faint tail.
A field of orbital debris surrounds {world}, left by impacts, broken moons or wrecked craft. Navigation near {world} requires current charts of the field.
Incomplete arcs of ring material circle {world}, held in place by the gravity of small moons. From some angles they appear as bright crescents against the sky.
A faint ring of fine dust surrounds {world}, visible only with the star behind it. The dust is replenished by impacts on the inner moons.
Belts of trapped charged particles encircle {world}, intense enough to damage unshielded craft that pass through them. Orbits around the world are chosen to avoid the belts.
{World} has no significant magnetic field, and the stellar wind strikes its upper atmosphere or surface directly. Radiation at the surface is correspondingly high.
{World} crosses streams of debris at fixed points in its orbit, producing meteor showers that light its night sky for days at a time. The heaviest showers carry a small risk to orbital installations.
Swarms of small bodies share {world's} orbit, gathered at the stable points ahead of and behind it. They are a ready source of ice and rock for orbital construction.
{World} lies in a system with two suns, and both appear in its sky, rising and setting at different times through the year.
Three suns cross {world's} sky, and full darkness comes only when all three have set.
{World's} sun is dim and red, and daylight on the surface is like a permanent dusk to eyes adjusted to brighter stars.
{World's} sun burns blue-white and very bright, and its light is harsh, with strong ultraviolet.
{World's} sun is a swollen giant that fills a large part of the sky, its disc visibly mottled and its light red or orange.
{World's} sun is a flare star, and its sudden flares brighten the sky and raise radiation at the surface without warning.
A pulsar flickers in {world's} sky, and the radiation it sweeps across the system can be measured at the surface.
{World} has no sun. Its sky is dark at all hours, lit only by distant stars and by whatever light the world itself produces.
{World's} sky is filled by the glow of a surrounding nebula, bright enough to light the surface faintly at night.
Neighboring stars of the Basin shine brightly in {world's} night sky, several bright enough to cast shadows.
The stars of the Lantern Reach are visible in {world's} sky, and their brightening and dimming on the seventy-three-day cycle is plainly seen.
Eclipses of {world's} sun by moons or companion bodies are frequent, and daylight is interrupted several times in a typical month.
{World's} sky is an unusual color, tinted by the chemistry of its atmosphere or the light of its star.
{World's} rings cast a broad shadow across the surface, and the band beneath them has a markedly colder climate than the latitudes around it.
A storm larger than many planets persists in {world's} atmosphere and has remained in place for years. It dominates the appearance of {world} and the weather around it.
features.example: Halvard's great storm has not moved in twelve years of observation.

features.description: Cloud covers {world} without a break, and its star is never seen from the surface. Light at ground level is diffuse and shadowless.
{World's} atmosphere circles the planet faster than its surface rotates, sustaining strong winds at all latitudes and carrying weather around the globe in a matter of days.
Dust storms recur on {world}, raising fine particles that cover regions or, at times, the entire planet for weeks. Visibility and solar power fall sharply while they last.
Rain on {world} is acidic and attacks exposed metal, stone and organic material. Structures and equipment require protective coatings or regular replacement.
Lightning strikes {world} at many times the rate of temperate planets, and electrical activity in its storms is a hazard to aircraft and unshielded equipment.
A persistent haze, photochemical or volcanic in origin, hangs in {world's} atmosphere. It colors the sky, softens the light at the surface and limits visibility at long range.
Cold, dense winds pour off {world's} high ice and plateaus and down into its lowlands, reaching great strength where valleys channel them.
Part of {world's} atmosphere freezes onto the surface in winter and returns to the air in summer, so that surface pressure changes considerably through the year.
{World's} clouds are organized into distinct bands parallel to the equator, driven by fast zonal winds. The bands are visible from orbit and shift slowly over the years.
Dense fog forms regularly over {world's} coasts and lowlands, persisting for days in calm weather. Visibility in the fog falls to a few meters.
Wildfires burn across large areas of {world} in the dry season, ignited by lightning and spread by wind. Native vegetation recovers quickly, but settlements and stores must be protected.
Severe storms on {world} produce hail large enough to damage crops, vehicles and unprotected structures.
{World} has a cyclone season each year, during which tropical storms form over warm seas and strike the coasts with high winds and flooding.
{World's} atmosphere admits strong ultraviolet light, and unprotected skin and materials suffer damage under open sky. Settlers wear covering outdoors, and plastics degrade in the sun.
Heavy gases collect in {world's} valleys, caves and craters, forming invisible pockets of unbreathable or toxic air. Low ground is entered only with monitoring equipment.
{World's} atmosphere is unusually calm, with light winds and little weather. Pollution, dust and smoke linger near their sources.
{World's} upper atmosphere glows faintly at night, so that the night sky is never fully dark.
A great mountain range on {world} blocks the prevailing winds, leaving the land on its lee side in a deep rain shadow that is much drier than the coast it faces.
Seasons on {world} are extreme, with summers far hotter and winters far colder than on most settled worlds.
Seasons on {world} are mild and barely distinguishable, and the climate changes little through the year.
{World's} polar regions spend months in continuous darkness in winter and continuous daylight in summer.
{World} is in an ice age, with ice sheets advanced far toward the equator and sea levels low.
{World's} climate is warming measurably, with ice retreating and sea levels rising over the period of observation.
{World's} climate is cooling measurably, with winters lengthening and ice advancing over the period of observation.
{World's} climate swings unpredictably between years, with droughts, floods and hard winters following one another without pattern.
{World's} poles are free of permanent ice, and its climate is warm enough at high latitudes to support forest.
Great rivers drain {world's} continents, thousands of kilometers long and navigable far inland. They carry most of the traffic and support most of the settlement.
A large inland sea occupies a basin on {world}, cut off from the ocean and saltier or fresher than it according to climate.
Glaciers fill {world's} mountain valleys and descend toward the lowlands, feeding rivers with meltwater through the summer.
Permanent ice caps cover {world's} poles, holding a large share of its water.
Hot springs rise on {world} wherever water meets heat from below, surrounded by mineral terraces and steam.
Pools of dense brine lie in {world's} low ground, colored by the microorganisms that live in them and lethal to most other life.
Deep aquifers lie beneath {world's} surface, holding water from a wetter past. They are not being replenished.
{World} has no standing water at its surface, and any water present is frozen, bound in minerals or deep underground.
{World's} seas are acidic, dissolving metal and carbonate rock and supporting only specially adapted life.
Alkaline soda lakes lie in {world's} closed basins, caustic to the touch and often colored pink or red by their inhabitants.
Tidal bores run up {world's} rivers with each high tide, walls of water that travel far inland against the current.
Strong tidal currents in {world's} narrow straits produce permanent whirlpools that are dangerous to shipping.
{World's} rivers flood across their plains each year, depositing fresh silt and drowning anything built too low.
Rivers flow underground across much of {world}, through caves and porous rock, and surface only at springs.
Sea ice covers {world's} oceans at high latitudes for much of the year, breaking up and refreezing with the seasons.

Tidal flexing by {world's} parent or a close companion heats its interior. The heat drives volcanism or keeps subsurface liquid from freezing, and {world} is geologically more active than its size would suggest.
Volcanoes on {world} are active, and eruptions occur somewhere on its surface every year. Fresh lava fields, ash deposits and volcanic gases are features of the landscape.
Volcanoes on {world} erupt water, ammonia or methane rather than molten rock, building domes and flows of ice and sometimes venting material into space.
Geysers erupt from {world's} surface, venting water or other volatiles in jets that may rise far above the ground. They are concentrated along zones of geological stress or heat.
A body of liquid water lies beneath {world's} surface, insulated by rock or ice. Its depth and extent are known only approximately, and it may host life of its own.
A large moon or close parent raises tides of many meters on {world}, flooding and exposing broad areas of coast twice in each cycle and driving strong currents through narrow channels.
A single impact basin hundreds of kilometers across dominates one hemisphere of {world}, its rim forming a ring of mountains and its floor a broad, low plain.
A canyon system on a continental scale cuts across {world}, many times deeper and longer than the largest canyons on settled Union worlds.
Strong earthquakes are frequent on {world}, and construction must be designed to withstand them. Fault lines and fresh scarps mark its surface.
Extensive natural cave systems run beneath {world's} surface, offering shelter from its climate and radiation and providing access to its interior.
Surface gravity on {world} is well below Union standard. Long residence weakens bone and muscle, but launches to orbit are cheap and heavy loads are easily moved.
Areas of {world's} surface have been fused into glass by an extreme heating event. The glass is flat, smooth and nearly featureless, cracked into plates by cooling.
{World's} crust is divided into moving plates, and earthquakes, volcanism and mountain-building are concentrated along their boundaries.
{World's} interior has cooled and its crust no longer moves. There is no volcanism and almost no seismic activity, and the surface changes only through impact and erosion.
Long rift valleys split {world's} crust where it is being pulled apart, their floors lying far below the surrounding plateaus and lined with volcanoes and lakes.
Mountain ranges on {world} rise far higher than those of settled Union worlds, their peaks above most of the atmosphere and their glaciers feeding the lowlands.
Broad shield volcanoes rise on {world}, some hundreds of kilometers across, built over long periods by fluid lava. Their slopes are gentle and their summit calderas vast.
A supervolcano lies beneath {world's} surface, marked by a caldera tens of kilometers across, hot springs and ground that rises and falls. An eruption would affect the climate of the whole world.
Sinkholes open without warning on {world} where the ground above caves and dissolved rock collapses. Construction requires survey of the ground beneath it.
Ground across large parts of {world} is unstable, subject to subsidence, slumping and sudden collapse. Foundations must be deep or flexible.
Steep slopes on {world} are prone to landslides, triggered by rain, quakes or thaw. Valleys and roads are regularly cut.
Caverns beneath {world's} surface are lined with large crystals grown from mineral-rich water over long periods, some several meters long.
Broad salt flats lie across {world's} lowlands, left by the evaporation of former lakes and seas. They are firm, flat and bright under the sun.
Seas of sand dunes cover large regions of {world}, moving slowly downwind and burying whatever lies in their path.
{World's} surface is extremely old and has changed little in billions of years, preserving a record of its early history that younger worlds have lost.
A recent large impact has scarred {world}, leaving a fresh crater, a field of ejecta and debris still settling in its atmosphere or orbit.
Permanently frozen ground underlies much of {world's} surface, and construction must be designed to avoid thawing it.
Strong local magnetic anomalies on {world} disturb compasses and simple instruments, and some correspond to concentrations of metal or buried structures.
Flash floods fill {world's} dry channels within minutes of distant rain, and camps are never pitched in a dry bed.
Avalanches of snow, ice or rock sweep {world's} mountain slopes, especially in spring and after storms.
{World's} dust is toxic, chemically or physically, and must be kept out of habitats and lungs.
Large eruptions on {world} periodically fill the atmosphere with ash and sulfur, cooling the surface for years and failing harvests.
Native diseases on {world} affect humans, and settlers depend on vaccination and medical stores.
Unexploded ordnance from past fighting lies across parts of {world}, and contested ground is dangerous to cross even after the fighting ends.
Blowing snow on {world} produces whiteouts in which ground and sky become indistinguishable, and travelers are lost within sight of shelter.
Quakes and landslides on {world} raise tsunamis that strike its coasts without warning.
Underground workings on {world} are prone to collapse, and mining there carries a high casualty rate.
Patches of quicksand, mud or fluid regolith on {world} trap people and vehicles that cross them.
{World} has an indigenous biosphere. Native life may be simple or complex, but it predates human arrival and is subject to the Charter's native-life protections.
Native life on {world} is limited to microorganisms. There are no native plants or animals, but microbial mats and films may cover large areas and alter the chemistry of air and water.
{World} supports native animals large enough to threaten a frame. Predators of this size make the open country dangerous and require settlements to be defended.
features.example: Verdance's predators are the standard example.

features.description: Native life on {world} poses a serious hazard to settlers through pathogens, toxins, parasites or aggressive predators. Settlement requires medical precautions and perimeter defense.
Native organisms on {world} construct large structures from stone, soil or their own secretions.
features.example: On Cairn, colonial organisms build stone structures several meters high that are observed to move.

features.description: Native life on {world} is under review for possible sapience under the Charter's native-life protections. A finding of sapience would void claims on {world} and restrict access to it.
Large herds of native grazing animals range across {world's} open country, moving with the seasons and supporting the predators that follow them.
Native organisms on {world} gather in vast swarms at certain seasons, darkening the sky or covering the ground as they move.
{World} supports large native predators at the top of its food chain. They are territorial and treat settlers and livestock as prey.
{World's} seas hold native animals of great size, some larger than any vessel that sails on them.
Native life on {world} has taken to the air in unusual abundance and variety, from drifting gas-filled organisms to large fliers.
{World's} native life is bound together by extensive symbiosis, so that organisms of very different kinds depend on one another for survival. The loss of one species can bring down many.
Life on {world} draws its energy from chemical reactions rather than sunlight, concentrated around vents, seeps and mineral deposits.
{World's} native life is built on a biochemistry incompatible with human digestion, and none of it can be eaten. Food must be grown from imported stock or shipped in.
Much of {world's} native life is edible to humans after simple preparation, and native crops and game supplement imported agriculture.
Species introduced by settlers have escaped cultivation on {world} and are spreading at the expense of native life.
Crops and livestock brought by settlers grow well on {world}, and imported agriculture has displaced native vegetation in the settled regions.
{World} preserves a rich fossil record of its earlier life in its sedimentary rock, of considerable interest to the Survey Office.
{World} once supported a biosphere that is now extinct. Fossils, preserved remains and altered soils record life that no longer exists.
Social organisms on {world} live in colonies of vast size, building nests, mounds or tunnels that cover large areas.
Much of {world's} native fauna is venomous, and bites and stings are a routine hazard for settlers working outdoors.
Native parasites on {world} can infect humans and livestock, and settlers follow strict precautions with water, food and exposed skin.
Life on {world} extends kilometers below the surface, in rock pores, aquifers and caves, and may outweigh the life above ground.
{World} holds rich deposits of iron, nickel and other common metals at accessible depths.
Deposits of rare-earth elements occur on {world}, valued for electronics and printer feed.
{World} holds workable deposits of radioactive elements, useful for power and dangerous to mine.
Precious and platinum-group metals occur on {world} in quantities worth extracting.
{World} holds large reserves of water ice, a ready supply of water, oxygen and reaction mass.
{World} is rich in volatiles such as nitrogen, ammonia and carbon dioxide, useful for life support and chemistry.
Helium-3 can be skimmed from {world's} upper atmosphere, a valuable fuel for fusion drives.
{World's} water or atmosphere is unusually rich in deuterium, an easily extracted fuel.
Deposits of hydrocarbons on {world} provide chemical feedstock for plastics and fuel.
{World's} forests yield large quantities of timber, cut for building and export.
{World's} waters support productive fisheries, a major source of food for its settlements.
{World} has large areas of arable land suited to imported crops.
Wide grazing lands on {world} support herds of livestock or native animals managed for food.
Geothermal heat on {world} is close to the surface and easily tapped for power.
Native plants and fungi on {world} yield compounds of medical value, collected and studied by settlers and companies.
{World} produces chemical compounds found nowhere else, of interest to industry and the Survey Office alike.
Salvage on or around {world} supports a trade in recovered metal, parts and equipment.
Good building stone is plentiful on {world} and quarried widely for construction.

Absent machinery buried kilometers beneath {world's} surface regulates its air and climate. The structures were discovered by survey and are spaced in a pattern that has not been explained. All of the Basin's garden worlds appear to have them.
The Absent machinery regulating {world's} climate is failing. Parts of it have stopped entirely while others run erratically, and {world's} winters, storms and coastal surges grow worse each year.
Absent machinery warms {world} from outside its natural energy budget, keeping water liquid where it would otherwise freeze. Nobody has switched one off or explained how it works.
features.example: The rogue worlds of the Hollows are warmed in this way.

features.description: Structures built by the Absent stand on or near {world}: towers, platforms, shipyards or constructions of no recognizable purpose. Their age and function are unknown.
A repeating transmission of Absent origin is received from {world} or its vicinity at a fixed interval. Its content has not been deciphered, and its source has not been located.
Active Absent machines defend {world's} deep workings and attack anyone who digs too close, usually below about four hundred meters. Mining crews treat the depth as a boundary.
Absent platforms the size of cities stand on or float above {world's} surface at regular intervals. Their purpose is unknown; some have been occupied by settlers.
Towers of Absent construction stand on {world}, some more than a kilometer tall, empty and without visible entrances or function.
The ruins of an Absent shipyard lie in or near {world's} orbit: cradles and gantries kilometers long, mostly broken, some still holding unfinished frames.
Wreckage of Absent origin lies on {world} or in its orbit, made of alloys nobody can manufacture. Some of it may once have been ships.
A structure of Absent origin lies buried beneath {world's} surface, detected by survey but not yet reached or fully mapped.
An Absent structure orbits {world}, inert or of unknown activity, and has been charted but not entered.
Measurements of gravity on {world} show local anomalies that cannot be explained by the distribution of rock, as though dense or unusual structures lie below.
Visitors to parts of {world} report losing time: clocks and memories disagree by hours on their return. The effect has not been explained.
Absent machinery on {world} appears to be dormant rather than dead, registering faint power and occasional changes of state.
Some Absent wreckage on or near {world} still has power, showing on sensors as heat and, now and then, as light.
A sealed chamber of Absent construction has been found on {world}. Attempts to open it have so far failed.
Space around {world} is unusually clean of dust and debris, as though something keeps it swept.
Features on {world's} surface or in its orbit fall into regular geometric patterns that no natural process explains.
Lattice occurs on {world} in seams through the rock, much as quartz does, and is mined by seam crews. The work is well paid and dangerous.
Lattice coats parts of {world's} surface as thin crusts that appear to have been deposited from outside. The crusts are easy to strip and slow to replace.
Fine grains of lattice are suspended in {world's} air, ice or rings, enormous in total quantity but slow to gather in useful amounts.
{World's} rings are composed largely of lattice, among the purest deposits known.
features.example: Choir, in the Shoals, is the example; the local lane to it drifts so fast that no route holds for long.

features.description: Lattice occurs on {world} as nodules scattered through rock or regolith, small but easy to recover.
Loose fields of lattice drift in the space around {world}, gathered by shielded ships without any mining.
Fine grains of lattice are scattered through glassed or fused rock on {world}, recoverable only by crushing large volumes of glass.
Lattice on {world} occurs already refined, built into Absent wreckage or structures. It can be cut out and used directly.
Lattice on {world} regrows slowly where it has been removed, by a process nobody has explained.
{World's} accessible lattice has been largely worked out, and the remaining deposits are deep, thin or dangerous.
Miners who work lattice on {world} for long periods report hearing it. Listener communities have formed among the crews.
{World's} richest lattice lies deep, below the depth at which custodians become active, and is reached only at great risk.
A primary lane mouth lies within a short distance of {world}, and traffic through the lane passes close to it.
A drifting lane mouth wanders near {world}, its position changing from month to month and requiring a recent chart to find.
A picket watches the approaches to {world}, inspecting traffic and collecting levies.
A station orbits {world}, serving as its port and the main point of contact with the rest of the Basin.
Orbital guns cover the approaches to {world}, and no hostile fleet has yet tested them.
Orbital yards above {world} build, refit or break up ships.
Interference around {world} blinds sensors, and ships nearby cannot be tracked reliably.
The space around {world} is hazardous to navigation through debris, radiation or gravitational complexity, and pilots require local knowledge.
{World} lies on a busy route, and ships of many owners call there for fuel, cargo and repair.
Hidden anchorages near {world} are used by smugglers and others who prefer not to be inspected.
A survey beacon marks {world}, broadcasting its position and the claims registered on it.
The approaches to {world} are poorly charted, and much of its system has not been surveyed.
The remains of a failed or evacuated settlement stand on {world}, with structures, equipment and records left in place by those who departed.
{World} is under quarantine, closed to landing by order of the Survey Office or another authority. The quarantine is enforced unevenly, and unauthorized landings occur.
{World} is the site of recent or continuing fighting. Wrecked frames, fortifications, craters and unexploded ordnance mark the contested ground.
Wrecked ships, frames or structures lie on {world's} surface or in its orbit, the remains of accidents, battles or abandoned operations, and are worked by salvagers.
{World} is the seat of a government, and its capital is the center of administration for a wider region.
A city of considerable size stands on {world}, its largest settlement and the center of its trade.
A company town on {world} is owned and run by a single firm, which employs, houses and governs most of its people.
Mining camps are scattered across {world}, small, temporary and supplied from elsewhere.
A refinery on {world} processes ore, lattice or volatiles brought in from the surrounding region.
Homesteads are scattered across {world's} settled regions, held by families under Allotment claims or older grants.
Towns on {world} float on its waters, moored by cables or anchors and moving with the tides and seasons.
{World's} settlements are sealed against its environment, connected by tunnels and pressurized vehicles.
A research station on {world} studies its environment, its life or its Absent remains.
A survey camp on {world} is charting it for claims, lanes or resources.
A religious mission is established on {world}, serving settlers or seeking converts.
Refugees have settled on {world} in crowded, poorly supplied camps.
{World's} principal settlements are fortified, with walls, gun positions and garrisons.
{World} is under military occupation by an outside power.
An insurgency is active on {world}, fought by settler militias against the authority that claims it.
A force is under siege on {world}, cut off from supply and surrounded.
Claims on {world} are disputed between rival filers, companies or governments, and the dispute is unresolved.
Land and mineral claims on {world} are registered with the Allotment.
An abandoned town stands on {world}, its buildings intact and its people gone.
A crash site on {world} marks where a ship or lander came down, its wreckage still in place.
A memorial on {world} marks the dead of a disaster, battle or failed settlement.
{World} hosts a free port, where goods change hands without levy or inspection.
